title: Named Arguments and Argument Unpacking
learning_outcomes: Explain what named arguments and argument unpacking contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: named arguments.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Functions package behavior behind named inputs and return values. Clear parameter and return types, small responsibilities, and controlled side effects make code easier to reuse and test. In this lesson, focus on named arguments; then compare it with positional versus named arguments. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use named arguments and argument unpacking when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Functions package behavior behind named inputs and return values. Clear parameter and return types, small responsibilities, and controlled side effects make code easier to reuse and test. For named arguments and argument unpacking, begin with named arguments. Also distinguish positional versus named arguments; variadic unpacking; array unpacking. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
